verification.notes: Provisional offline teaching fixture; no independent Korean review or audio assessment.

units.phonology: The final ㄱ of 국 is followed by the nasal ㅁ of 물, so ㄱ becomes the nasal ㅇ: [궁물]. The learner cue gung-mul reflects that change.
units.structure: A two-noun compound: 국 (soup) plus 물 (water or liquid). Korean compounds do not need an English-style possessive marker.
units.register: Everyday neutral noun; usable in polite speech.
units.translation_note: English usually says soup or broth; the literal compound image is soup water.
units.dialect_note: Standard pronunciation example; no regional claim.

units.phonology: The final ㄱ of 국 meets the nasal ㅁ of 말 and becomes ㅇ: [한궁말].
units.structure: 한국 (Korea) plus 말 (speech or language). The compound is understood as one noun.
units.register: Neutral and slightly colloquial; 한국어 is often preferred in formal writing.
units.translation_note: English says Korean language. 말 stresses speech, while 어 is a more formal bound word for language.
units.dialect_note: Standard-language example; regional vocabulary is not assessed here.

units.english: Is, am, or are (formal polite copula).
units.phonology: The final ㅂ of 입 is followed by ㄴ and becomes ㅁ: [임니다].
units.structure: The copula 입니다 attaches to a noun in the formal polite 합니다 style.
units.register: Formal polite; common in presentations, announcements, and service encounters.
units.translation_note: English supplies a be verb; Korean often omits a clear subject and relies on context.
units.dialect_note: Standard formal register; no dialect comparison.

units.phonology: The final ㅂ of 십 meets the nasal ㅁ and becomes ㅁ: [심만].
units.structure: Sino-Korean number: 십 (ten) times 만 (ten thousand), giving one hundred thousand.
units.translation_note: English groups large numbers by thousands; Korean groups them by ten-thousands.
units.dialect_note: Standard number reading; no regional variant claimed.

units.phonology: The final ㅇ of 종 is followed by ㄹ, and ㄹ becomes the nasal ㄴ: [종노].
units.structure: A place-name compound of 종 and 로. Its conventional pronunciation is lexical.
units.translation_note: English uses the transliteration Jongno rather than a meaning-based translation.
units.dialect_note: This is the standard name and pronunciation for the Seoul district.
units.literal_english: Bell street, from historical components; not a current translation.

exercises.prompt: How is 국물 pronounced in connected speech?
Choose the connected-speech form of 한국말.
The final ㅂ in 입니다 becomes which sound before ㄴ?

verification.notes: Provisional offline teaching fixture; no independent Korean review or audio assessment.

units.phonology: The final ㅁ of 음 moves to the empty initial position of 악, giving [으막].
units.structure: A Sino-Korean noun. In isolation it needs no particle; sentence roles use particles.
units.translation_note: English music is a direct equivalent; no article is needed in Korean.

units.phonology: The final ㄱ of 국 moves before the vowel 어: [한구거]. It is no longer a final consonant.
units.structure: 한국 (Korea) plus 어, a bound Sino-Korean word for language.
units.register: Neutral to formal; 한국말 is more conversational.
units.translation_note: English Korean language. Korean can combine two roots without a space.
units.dialect_note: Standard-language example; regional vocabulary is outside this fixture.

units.phonology: The final ㅅ of 옷 moves to the vowel 이, producing [오시].
units.structure: 옷 (clothes) plus 이, the subject marker used after a consonant.
units.translation_note: English marks subjects by word order; Korean often marks them with a particle.
units.dialect_note: Standard particle form; no dialect claim.

units.english: A flower, with the object particle.
units.phonology: The final ㅊ of 꽃 moves before the vowel 을: [꼬츨].
units.structure: 꽃 (flower) plus 을, the object marker used after a consonant.
units.translation_note: The object particle has no separate English word; English shows the role by position.
units.dialect_note: Standard particle form; no regional claim.

units.english: Rice or a meal, with the object particle.
units.phonology: The final ㅂ of 밥 moves before the vowel 을: [바블].
units.structure: 밥 (rice or meal) plus 을, the object marker after a consonant.
units.translation_note: English meal or rice depends on context; the Korean noun covers both.
units.dialect_note: Standard particle form; no regional claim.

title: Aspiration: ㅎ combines with plain consonants

verification.notes: Provisional offline teaching fixture; no independent Korean review or audio assessment.

units.phonology: The final ㅎ of 좋 combines with the following ㄷ to make ㅌ: [조타].
units.structure: A dictionary-form adjective. Stem 좋- takes endings such as -아요 or -습니다.
units.translation_note: English good is an adjective; Korean adjectives also conjugate for tense and politeness.

units.phonology: The final ㄱ of 축 meets ㅎ and becomes aspirated ㅋ: [추카].
units.structure: A Sino-Korean noun. It commonly appears with 합니다 or 드립니다 in polite formulas.
units.translation_note: English congratulations is plural in form; Korean 축하 is a noun.

units.phonology: The final ㅂ of 입 combines with ㅎ to make ㅍ: [이팍].
units.structure: Sino-Korean 입 (enter) plus 학 (study or school).
units.translation_note: English can say school admission or entering school; Korean uses one noun.

units.english: To seat someone; to set something down.
units.phonology: The final cluster of 앉 leaves ㄴ, while ㅈ combines with ㅎ to make ㅊ: [안치다].
units.structure: Causative 앉- (sit) plus the causative suffix -히-.
units.translation_note: English uses a separate causative verb; Korean adds a causative suffix.

units.phonology: The final ㄷ of 맏 combines with ㅎ to make aspirated ㅌ: [마텽].
units.structure: 맏 (eldest) plus 형 (older brother). Kinship terms depend on the speaker and relationship.
units.register: Familiar kinship term, usually used by a male speaker for an older brother.
units.translation_note: English eldest brother is descriptive; Korean kinship terms also encode age and relationship.
units.dialect_note: Standard kinship term; regional usage may vary.

verification.notes: Provisional offline teaching fixture; no independent Korean review or audio assessment.

units.phonology: The final ㄱ of 학 is followed by another ㄱ, and the second becomes tense ㄲ: [학꾜].
units.structure: Sino-Korean 학 (study) plus 교 (school).
units.translation_note: English school maps directly to the Korean compound; no article is used.

units.phonology: The final ㅂ of 밥 is followed by ㅅ, and ㅅ becomes tense ㅆ: [밥쌍].
units.structure: 밥 (rice or meal) plus 상 (table).
units.translation_note: English dining table is natural; the literal image is a rice table.

units.english: To exist, to have, or to be located.
units.phonology: The tense final ㅆ of 있 is followed by ㄷ, and ㄷ becomes tense ㄸ: [읻따].
units.structure: An existential verb. It also appears in possession and progressive constructions.
units.register: Neutral verb used across polite registers.
units.translation_note: English have, exist, or be located depends on the construction; Korean uses 있다 in several patterns.

units.phonology: The final ㄹ of 갈 is followed by ㄷ, and ㄷ becomes tense ㄸ: [갈뜽].
units.structure: A Sino-Korean noun used for interpersonal or social conflict.
units.translation_note: English conflict is broader; Korean 갈등 often suggests tension between parties.
units.literal_english: Tangled vines, from historical components; current meaning is conflict.

units.phonology: The final ㄱ of 식 is followed by ㄷ, and ㄷ becomes tense ㄸ: [식땅].
units.structure: Sino-Korean 식 (eat) plus 당 (hall or building).
units.translation_note: English restaurant is natural; the literal compound is eating hall.

title: Palatalisation: ㄷ and ㅌ before 이

verification.notes: Provisional offline teaching fixture; no independent Korean review or audio assessment.

units.phonology: The final ㅌ of 같 becomes ㅊ before the vowel 이: [가치].
units.structure: An adverb formed from the adjective 같- with the adverbial suffix -이.
units.translation_note: English together is not a literal gloss of like; the Korean form is lexicalized.

units.phonology: The final ㄷ of 굳 becomes ㅈ before the vowel 이: [구지].
units.structure: An adverb from the adjective 굳- plus the adverbial suffix -이.
units.translation_note: English has several context-dependent equivalents; no single gloss covers every use.

units.phonology: The final ㄷ of 닫 meets the suffix 히, and ㄷ plus ㅎ becomes ㅊ: [다치다].
units.structure: Passive 닫- (close) plus the passive suffix -히-.
units.translation_note: English can use passive be closed or active close; Korean uses a passive suffix.

units.phonology: The final ㅌ of 붙 becomes ㅊ before the vowel 이: [부치다].
units.structure: Transitive or causative 붙- (stick) plus the suffix -이-.
units.translation_note: English attach or stick is transitive; Korean marks the change with a suffix.

units.phonology: The final ㄷ of 돋 becomes ㅈ before the vowel 이: [해도지].
units.structure: 해 (sun) plus 돋- (rise) plus the nominalizing suffix -이.
units.translation_note: English sunrise is a noun; Korean builds it from sun, rise, and a nominalizer.
